newsitem.title: THAILAND: FEATURE - Depressed Thai property heading down but not out.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Depressed Thai property heading down but not out.

text.p: Conditions in the sickly Thai property sector will worsen further but prospects of falling prices and steady demand mean the market's long term prognosis is far from terminal, analysts say.

"Markets go through cycles and this is part of one. We really have not had much of a cycle in Thailand before, it's been pretty much one way traffic," said Craig Plumb, research manager at property firm Jones Lang Wootton.

The cycle is most definitely down, with growing oversupply, a slowdown in economic growth and high interest rates threatening the future of developers and their creditors, property executives and analysts told Reuters.

To top it all, problems in the property sector have spilt over to local financial institutions who have lent billions of dollars over the years to cash-strapped developers now hit by liquidity crunches and unable to repay, they said.
OVERSUPPLY REACHING CRITICAL LEVELS
According to the property firm Chestertons, supply in the office and retail sectors in Bangkok has increased by more than 400 percent over the last six years.

New demand for office space in 1996 was around 550,000 square metres while supply was 600,000 square metres. Office space supply will increase by an average one million square metres per year to 2001, Jones Lang Wootton said.
Similar problems exist in the residential market where some private sector firms estimate 600,000 units stand empty.
The condominium market has been hardest hit and private sector research suggests it will take three years at current demand levels to absorb the existing 12,500 unsold units.
In the retail sector vacancy rates in the overstocked sector rose to 14 percent in 1996, double the 1995 rate, property firm Richard Ellis said in a recent report.
LIMITING DAMAGE TO THE FINANCIAL SYSTEM

The Thai economy grew at a rate of 6.8 percent last year, its lowest level for a decade. With interest rates among the highest in Asia at over 13 percent the oversupply situation has left highly-geared developers facing a liquidity crunch.
Medium-sized property firm Somprasong Land became the first Thai company to default on a Eurobond interest payment in February when it failed to honour a $3.1 million obligation.
The default added to fears that developers facing similar problems would fail to honour debts to local finance firms which have extended around 400 billion baht ($15.4 billion) to developers.
Finance firms have extended an average 25 percent of their total loans to the real estate sector, or around half the sector's total 800 billion credit, the central bank estimates.
Growing concern about the likely deterioration of the quality of the finance sector's loans, and the possible damage defaults could inflict on the finance sector saw the government step in.
At the begining of March it proposed a 100 billion baht ($3.85 billion) issue of seven year zero coupon bonds which will relieve finance firms of some of their low quality loans.
"The pin had been inserted into the property bubble and was about to be pulled out. The Thai government is trying to keep it in," said one foreign analyst.
STEADY DEMAND AND CHEAPER PRICES

"With relatively few exceptions property values have remained static for the last four years or even fallen in real terms," said a recent Chulalongkorn University report on the Bangkok property market.

According to Richard Ellis research, Bangkok office space is now among the cheapest in Asia. Prime office freehold normally sells at between 55,000-70,000 baht per square metre while rentals vary between 280-550 baht per square metre per month.
Cheap prices are generating interest from foreign buyers, but with the market set to weaken further they are waiting for bargains to appear, analysts said.

"I've personally met two people from the U.S. and Singapore but they are just watching. There is a belief that prices may have fallen as much as 30 percent over the last year," said Vikas Kawatra, property analyst at Asia Equity.
With current activity in the market, results of assets valuations on defaulter Somprasong due later this month are eagerly awaited as a true price indicator, executives said.

"There is a feeling that the market has yet to find its true value...The prices being asked at the moment have quite a lot of fat on them, we haven't reached a stage yet where people are offering prices at below cost," Plumb said.
LONG TERM CYCLE SHOULD TURN UP

The Thai economy is unlikely to repeat the sky high growth rates of earlier years, but the economy should still grow around five to six percent this year and demand for property should remain strong in the longer term, analysts said.
"The strength of demand will continue to underlie good projects and good projects will continue to attract tenants," Plumb said.
If demand rises as expected, all sectors should reach an equilibrium with slowing supply growth within five years.

While that will almost certainly be too late to save some cash-strapped developers from failure, it is an evolution of a market which offers strong prospects for those able to weather the current storm.
"Five years is a very long time but some of the really good developers should emerge to have a good time. There will be some clear winners emerging from this," Asia Equity's Kawatra said.
($ = 25.96 Thai Baht)
